KEY MESSAGE 1...Strengthening coastal low brings a period of
moderate to heavy rainfall late today into early Monday 
morning with the potential for typical brief nuisance street 
flooding. 

Low pressure will deepen as it tracks northward toward southern
New England late today into early Monday morning. Within this 
amplified flow, a plume of above normal moisture, 290-330 
percent of normal, surges northward ahead of the approaching 
trough and coastal low. This will prime the environment for 
heavy rainfall once the better forcing/instability arrive with 
the low. Models have also come into better agreement with the 
track of the low which should likely track to the east of Cape 
Cod and the Islands overnight into early Monday am. 
High res guidance paints the greatest chance for heavier 
rainfall across the urban areas of SE MA and RI. This includes 
rather flood-prone cities like New Bedford and Fall River. The 
saving grace that will likely prevent widespread flash flooding 
is the progressive nature of the system. Still, high-res models 
show a quick 1-3" of rainfall tonight into early Mon am with 
the majority of those totals falling in a roughly 6 hour window.
The aforementioned PWAT values (in this case around 1.8-2") and
ample frontal forcing may allow for some rather prolific 
rainfall rates Sunday night. However, again, given the 
progressive nature of the system, flash flood risk is low, 
although can't rule out ponding of water or urban/poor drainage 
flooding. 

A period of gusty winds will likely accompany the low as it moves 
over the eastern part of our CWA and strengthens as it quickly moves 
NE into the Gulf of Maine later Sunday night. Aloft, a 50-60 kt low 
level jet develops at 925 mb on the eastern side of low pressure. 
Guidance has nudged slightly further E with the latest update which 
will help to limit the strongest gusts to areas SE of I-95. 
Another limiting factor is the fact that the strongest LLJ moves
in overnight, a nighttime inversion should limit the full 
degree of mixing of the 50-60 kt gusts to the surface. Gusts 
likely range 25-40 mph with the strongest winds/gusts near the 
Cape and Islands. With the slight eastward trend in the low 
center, ensemble probabilities of wind gusts >40 mph have 
decreased to between 30 and 50 percent and the higher end of 
these values are more confined to the Cape and Islands. Thus, 
while the threat for heavy rain has remained relatively 
unchanged since the last update, the chance of strong or 
damaging winds has diminished. Another burst of gusty winds 
arrives Monday morning and afternoon as moderate cold air 
advection develops behind departing low pressure. A modest low 
level jet develops allowing 925 mb winds increase to between 30 
and 35 kts so opted to blend the NBM90th guidance in to increase
inland winds especially across the higher terrain.

Despite the rising astronomical tides, the quick moving system 
shouldn't bring major coastal flooding impacts. Most coastal flood 
guidance shows a modest surge of around 1 to 1.5 feet around Monday 
morning's high tide but at that point the greatest pressure falls 
and onshore winds have subsided. At the time of Monday's high tide, 
winds will have likely shifted more to the west and pressures will 
be rising so any lingering excess tide departure would be quick to 
move out. As a result, think impacts will likely be limited to 
splashover and perhaps very minor coastal flooding for the Mon high 
tide along the east coast, Cape, and Nantucket. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...Dry & colder weather follows Tue into Wed with highs 
mainly in   the 40s. Lows Tue night mainly in the upper teens & 20s. 

Dry but colder air will work into the region behind the departing 
coastal storm Tue into Wed. Modest cold advection with 925T dropping 
to between -2C/-3C should hold highs Tue and Wed mainly in the 
40s...But parts of the highest terrain may only see highs reach the 
upper 30s. It will be a bit breezy on Tue but high pressure overhead 
should result in rather light winds for Wed. It will be quite cold 
Tue night with an ideal night of radiational cooling. Lows Tue night 
will probably be mainly in the upper teens and 20s with even 
downtown Boston likely dropping between 30 and 32 degrees. Probably 
the coldest weather of the season so far for many locations.

KEY MESSAGE 3...Potential for impactful coastal storm Thanksgiving 
into Friday. Strong winds along the coast/coastal flooding are the 
greatest concerns given very high astronomical tides. Dangerous 
conditions possible for mariners as well. Ptype will be mainly a 
windswept rain...although a low risk for a brief period of snow/ice 
across the very distant interior high terrain.
